title: Don't explain their pain (Job 4–5)
hookLine: the friends insist the innocent never suffer
carry: the book won't let it fit
tomorrow: I would speak to the Almighty

cards: "Everything happens for a reason." It gets said at hospital bedsides and after funerals, by kind people who want to help. Eliphaz, the first friend to speak, is that kind of person.

He starts gently, almost apologizing: "If we assay to commune with thee, wilt thou be grieved? but who can withhold himself from speaking?" In plain words: I know this might hurt, but I can't keep quiet.
He reminds Job that he's comforted others, strengthened weak hands, steadied stumbling knees. Now it's come to you, he says, and you're shaken. Then he asks his real question.

teach.b: "Remember, I pray thee, who ever perished, being innocent? or where were the righteous cut off?" Name one innocent person who was ever destroyed. You can't.

teach.h: THEY THAT PLOW INIQUITY REAP IT.
teach.b: He backs it with what he's seen: "they that plow iniquity, and sow wickedness, reap the same."
He even describes a vision in the night, a spirit gliding past his face, his hair standing up, a whisper asking whether any mortal can be more just than God.
By chapter five he offers hope on the same terms: "Behold, happy is the man whom God correcteth." Take the correction, and you'll be restored.

Much of this sounds like wisdom you could hear anywhere: good things grow from good seeds; God is greater than we are. But he's saying it to a man in ashes, scraping his skin, whose children are dead.

teach.h: A GENERAL TRUTH, AIMED AT ONE MAN.
teach.b: Aimed at him, every general truth becomes an accusation: you must have done something.
And we know what Eliphaz doesn't. Chapter one told us Job is perfect and upright, and his suffering began with a question asked in heaven, not with anything he did.
Eliphaz has a theory that explains the world, and he needs Job's suffering to fit it. The book won't let it fit. At the very end, God will say the friends haven't spoken rightly.
Notice how the explaining starts: kindly, reasonably, from a friend who sat in silence for seven days.

how: Jewish teaching on comforting mourners, drawn partly from Job's friends, warns against explaining a death or a loss to the bereaved; visitors are encouraged to listen and let the mourner lead.

o: Job's eldest son, lost when the house fell
the messenger who brings Job the bad news
the first of Job's friends to answer him

s: Eliphaz starts out shouting at Job
he starts gently: if we try to speak with you, will you be grieved?
Eliphaz says Job has never helped anyone
he says the opposite: Job has strengthened weak hands and steadied stumbling knees.
Eliphaz says the innocent never perish

games.q: you're Eliphaz. you've sat in silence with Job for seven days, and now he's cursed the day he was born. what do you do?
o: explain that the innocent never perish, so he should accept correction.
agree that his suffering makes no sense.
games.why: he speaks, kindly at first, then asks who ever perished being innocent. the book won't let Job's suffering fit his theory.

practice: Remember a time someone explained your pain to you, maybe kindly, it was meant to be, at least you have, God doesn't give you more than you can handle, and notice how it landed; then, with no shame, a time you did it to someone else.
Think of one person hurting now, and try what you might say instead: I'm here, I'm so sorry, tell me. If you pray, you can pray for them without trying to make sense of it.

wordCard.voice: Eliphaz, the first of Job's friends to speak, who turns a kind question into an accusation that Job must have sinned. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: innocent, clean; the word in Eliphaz's question in Job 4:7.

carryVoice: Your line: the book won't let it fit. Eliphaz means well. That's day eight hundred forty-two.
